newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy metalworkers talks resume.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy metalworkers talks resume.

text.p: Unions and employers in Italy's key engineering and metalworking industry returned to the bargaining table on Monday and the government said it hoped the talks would lead to a rapid end to their bitter pay dispute.

But union leaders were cautious about the prospects for a swift deal, telling reporters that more than three hours of talks with the employers' group Federmeccanica had failed to resolve outstanding differences.
The unions, FIOM, FIM and UILM were scheduled to meet jointly on Monday night to review their position pending a fresh round of talks with Federmeccanica leaders on Tuesday morning.
"The climate is still the same. There are problems that still have not been resolved. Each side will study in the meantime to what extent they can be overcome," UILM leader Luigi Angeletti said.
Monday's talks were the first for more than a month in a battle that has seen three one-day strikes since it began last June.

They took place at the Labour Ministry after Prime Minister Romano Prodi met leaders of Italy's three main labour confederations, CGIL, CISL and UIL, and the employers' umbrella group Confindustria to try to break the deadlock.

"At the end of the meeting, by common agreement, it was decided to resume talks immediately among the parties at the Labour Ministry in order to reach a rapid conclusion to the dispute," a government statement said after Prodi's talks.
The dispute affects 1.7 million workers in a sector which accounts for 40 percent of Italy's industrial output.
Any deal is likely to set the tone for other pay settlements and prove key to Italy's hopes of keeping a lid on inflation.

Italian television, in an unsourced report, said negotiators would look at a compromise deal involving monthly wage rises of 180,000 to 200,000 lire ($113-$144) and a 30-month contract period rather than the standard two years.

The dispute centres on differing interpretations of a landmark 1993 accord between the labour confederations, Confindustria and the government that ended a system of automatic inflation-linked wage increases.

Unions in the industry, which includes Italy's biggest company Fiat, initially sought a 230,000 lire a month rise to compensate for lost purchasing power but accepted a government proposal of 200,000 lire in December.
Federmeccanica has so far stuck to its original offer of 139,000 lire, arguing that any more would raise labour costs and fuel inflation, now running at about 2.6 percent year-on-year.
Prodi has insisted the government's compromise proposal is not inflationary.

He called Monday's talks with Confindustria and the labour confederations last Friday after signs of movement in the dispute over the 1996-1998 contract period. The previous agreement covering the industry expired last June.
